strengths: Novel problem formulation and first comprehensive global-scale audio geolocation benchmark with new datasets (iNatSounds benchmark setup and XCDC with 576 species-rich recordings)

Well-designed experimental evaluation with clear baselines, clever species oracle experiments using SINR range maps providing informative upper bounds (97.8% region accuracy), and comprehensive ablations across components

Important insights identifying species identification as the critical bottleneck—the 95 percentage point gap between oracle (97.8%) and best method (17.2%) region accuracy clearly contextualizes fundamental challenges

Thorough experimental work with standard deviations across 3 runs, appropriate evaluation metrics across geographic scales, and honest treatment of limitations including geographic bias and distribution shift to XCDC
Extensive supplementary material supporting reproducibility with detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, and computation resources
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: AG-CLIP is a straightforward addition of a species checklist decoder to GeoCLIP; other methods are basic adaptations of existing approaches (regression, classification, retrieval); vision-inspired spectrogram approach is standard practice not justified over alternatives

Modest and limited performance with concerning generalization: 17.2% region accuracy on iNatSounds drops dramatically to 4.3% on species-rich XCDC, indicating poor generalization to natural multi-species scenarios despite same ecological domain

Fundamental bottleneck limits practical impact: paper demonstrates species identification is the binding constraint (2.5% vs 25.8% region accuracy with predicted vs true species on XCDC), but this is outside the scope and reduces real-world applicability

Underdeveloped multimodal geo-forensics component: only 4 movie clips with purely qualitative evaluation, no systematic analysis, no dataset created; divergences noted but not explained; feels like an afterthought that dilutes paper focus

Significant geographic bias with performance variation: iNatSounds heavily biased toward North America/Europe with clear spatial disparities (good performance in US/Europe, poor in Africa/Asia); distribution shift to XCDC suggests fundamental generalization issues

Paper tries to cover too much ground (core geolocation, species-rich recordings, spatiotemporal aggregation, multimodal forensics), weakening execution and focus; spatiotemporal aggregation experiments are artificial (year-long aggregation unrealistic in practice)

Overstated novelty claims: called 'first study' but primarily a benchmarking contribution building on existing image geolocation methods; earlier audio geolocation studies exist (refs 14, 25, 26, 40, 48)

Missing analysis of what signals AG-CLIP learns, auxiliary checklist loss provides only marginal improvements (2.7% at continent level), and limited investigation into failure modes despite spatial variation shown in results

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation for global-scale audio geolocation using wildlife sounds, which is relatively unexplored
Comprehensive systematic benchmarking of multiple geolocation formulations (regression, classification, species ranges, retrieval) with thorough ablations on encoders and temporal aggregation
Effective species oracle experiments demonstrating theoretical upper bounds (97.8% region accuracy) and showing the performance gap to practical methods
Multiple evaluation perspectives including distance thresholds across scales, spatial variation analysis, and CDF curves providing nuanced performance characterization
Detailed implementation details, commitment to releasing code and benchmark, and transparent discussion of limitations and geographic bias
New XCDC dataset of 576 species-rich dawn chorus recordings providing a resource for future research
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: AG-CLIP is primarily GeoCLIP plus auxiliary BCE loss for species checklists with minimal parameter increase (4.4M→4.7M), representing incremental rather than novel contribution

Critical unresolved distribution shift: severe performance collapse on XCDC species-rich recordings (4.3% vs 17.2% region accuracy), indicating models trained on short recordings fail to generalize to realistic multi-species scenarios

Species detection bottleneck remains unsolved: species-based approaches only achieve 2.5-9.3% accuracy, yet the paper provides no solutions beyond acknowledgment of the core hypothesis failing in practice

Modest absolute performance inadequate for applications: 17.2% region-level accuracy (200km threshold, roughly US state size) insufficient for practical geolocation, forensics, or authentication use cases

Insufficient analysis of model behavior: no interpretability investigation, error analysis, or explanation of what AG-CLIP learns beyond explicit species information; claims of implicit ambient sound usage lack evidence

Aggregation results show limited practical utility: improvements require unrealistic access to multiple recordings from same spatiotemporal neighborhood; performance degrades significantly with finer temporal windows, suggesting strong seasonal variation limitations

Geographic dataset bias inadequately addressed: acknowledged bias toward Western countries/Northern Hemisphere with no per-region performance analysis; method likely fails in underrepresented regions (Africa, South Asia)

Underdeveloped multimodal geo-forensics component: only 4 anecdotal movie examples with purely qualitative evaluation; movie audio is synthesized and differs fundamentally from natural recordings; unclear practical utility

Evaluation concerns: XCDC dataset too small (576 recordings) for robust evaluation; off-the-shelf baselines (GeoCLAP, Taxabind) not tuned for this task; naive baseline (1.1%) weak; no human performance baseline or statistical significance testing

Vision-inspired spectrogram approach not justified: no comparison with raw waveform or modern audio representations (wav2vec, CLAP); Table 2a results for these methods may reflect suboptimal configurations rather than fundamental limitations

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First systematic global-scale audio geolocation study with natural sounds, filling a clear gap in the literature
Comprehensive benchmarking: Multiple well-designed approaches (regression, classification, retrieval, species ranges) with proper baselines and ablations demonstrating thoughtful experimental design
Clear evaluation framework: Multiple distance thresholds (city/regional/country/continental) and appropriate metrics (Haversine distance) suitable for the task
Well-designed species oracle experiments: Clearly establish performance ceiling (97.8% region accuracy) and validate core hypothesis about species as geolocation signal

Honest and thorough reporting: Explicitly discusses limitations (geographic bias, XCDC generalization failure, species detection bottleneck) and provides extensive ablations and supplementary analysis
Reproducibility: Promises code and benchmark release, detailed hyperparameters, timing information, and comprehensive supplementary material enabling reproduction
Strong presentation: Clear motivation, excellent visualizations (especially Figure 1), well-organized structure, and proper contextualization within related work
weaknesses: XCDC generalization failure: Models trained on short iNatSounds recordings catastrophically underperform on species-rich XCDC audio (4.3% region vs 25.8% with true species), directly contradicting the paper's framing of species-rich audio as a key contribution and raising questions about the robustness of the approach

Unresolved species detection bottleneck: 23.5 percentage-point gap between predicted species (2.5% region) and ground truth species (25.8% region) on XCDC reveals that species classification, not geolocation itself, is the limiting factor. Paper identifies but doesn't address this fundamental constraint on practical deployment

Limited methodological novelty: Methods primarily adapt existing techniques (spectrograms with vision models, GeoCLIP location encoder, SINR species ranges). AG-CLIP is a straightforward combination of existing components with an auxiliary BCE loss

Moderate absolute performance: 17.2% region accuracy requires additional spatiotemporal aggregation to reach 30.4%, limiting utility for precise geolocation. Performance ceiling established by species oracles suggests inherent limitations of the audio signal

Geographic bias inadequately addressed: iNatSounds heavily biased toward Western countries and Northern Hemisphere. Spatial performance variation (Fig. 3) correlates with training data density rather than acoustic properties, limiting applicability to underrepresented regions despite acknowledgment
Small XCDC dataset: Only 576 recordings with larger error bars limit confidence in species-rich audio conclusions. Distribution shift from iNatSounds suggests generalization challenges
Preliminary multimodal geo-forensics: Section 5.4 analysis based on only 4 movies with anecdotal evaluation, feeling more exploratory than rigorous contribution
